lesson.title: The Rules That Keep Probability Honest
lesson.summary: A short list of rules, bounded values, a certain sample space, the complement rule, and the addition rule for disjoint events, is what every legitimate probability model must obey.
lesson.body:
Every legitimate way of assigning probabilities to outcomes has to obey the same short list of rules, no matter what the random phenomenon actually is. First, every probability is a number between 0 and 1, where 0 means an event never happens and 1 means it always happens; there is no such thing as a probability of 1.3 or negative 0.2, and any calculation that produces one has made an error somewhere upstream. Second, the probability of the entire sample space, meaning the probability that some outcome happens at all, is exactly 1, since a random phenomenon always produces some result even if which particular result is unpredictable. Third, the complement rule states that the probability an event does not happen equals 1 minus the probability that it does, written P(not A) = 1 minus P(A), because an event and its complement together account for every possible outcome with no overlap. Fourth, the addition rule for disjoint events states that if two events cannot happen on the same trial, the probability that one or the other happens is simply the sum of their individual probabilities.

These rules are not arbitrary bookkeeping, they are common sense about chance translated into arithmetic that can be checked. A probability of 1 for certainty and 0 for impossibility matches how everyone already thinks about sure things and impossible things. The complement rule matches the intuition that if there is a 30 percent chance of rain, there must be a 70 percent chance it does not rain, since those are the only two possibilities. The addition rule for disjoint outcomes matches the intuition that if a bag contains only red, blue, and green marbles with no marble being two colors at once, the chance of pulling red or blue is just the red chance plus the blue chance, since those two outcomes never compete for the same draw.

These rules are also useful as a diagnostic. If someone hands you a probability model where the numbers assigned to all outcomes add up to 1.15, or where one outcome is assigned a probability of negative 0.1, the model is simply wrong and cannot describe a real random phenomenon, regardless of how the numbers were generated. Checking that a set of probabilities obeys these rules is often the fastest way to catch an error before it propagates into a much bigger mistake.

A standard deck of 52 playing cards, split evenly into four 13 card suits, shows all four rules working together. The probability of drawing a heart is 13 out of 52, which reduces to one fourth, a number safely between 0 and 1. Applying the complement rule, the probability of not drawing a heart is 1 minus one fourth, or three fourths, which should equal the combined chance of drawing a spade, club, or diamond, and it does. Applying the addition rule to two disjoint events, drawing a heart and drawing a spade share no outcomes, since no card is both, so the probability of drawing a heart or a spade is 13/52 plus 13/52, which equals 26/52, or one half. Finally, adding the probability of all four suits together, four times 13/52, gives 52/52, which equals 1 exactly as the second rule requires, confirming the whole model is internally consistent.

The next several chapters each take one of these ideas and develop it in much greater depth: precisely defining the sample space a probability model is built on, formalizing what it means for events to be disjoint, and extending the addition rule to handle events that do overlap. Everything that follows is really just these same four rules, applied more carefully and to more interesting situations.
